entries.meaning: To make a file, app, or window appear on a screen so you can use it. ---
examples: Open the app and sign in with your email.
I opened the attachment and my laptop froze.
The file is opening - give it a second.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (open the app), intransitive (the file opens slowly)
entries.contrast: No doubled n: opened, opening. The stress is on the first syllable, so the consonant stays single.

entries.meaning: To make a file, window, or program stop being open. ---
examples: Close the other tabs to speed up the browser.
He closed the laptop without saving the file.
The app keeps closing on its own.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (close the window), intransitive (the app closed by itself)
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a z sound (KLOHZ). The adjective close, meaning near, ends in an s sound (KLOHS).

entries.meaning: To shrink a window down to the taskbar without closing it. ---
examples: Minimize the window instead of closing it.
She minimized the chat and went back to her spreadsheet.
He was minimizing every window one by one.
entries.contrast: American spelling uses -ize: minimize, minimized. British writing has minimise.

entries.meaning: To make a window fill the whole screen. ---
examples: Maximize the video before the call starts.
He maximized the window and the text got bigger.
I have maximized both windows and they still overlap.
entries.русский: разворачивать, развернуть (окно на весь экран); максимизировать

entries.meaning: To make a picture or a window bigger or smaller. ---
examples: Resize the photo before you upload it.
She resized the logo to fit the header.
I am resizing the window so both files fit.

entries.meaning: To load a page or a file again. ---
examples: Reload the page if the video will not play.
The browser reloaded and lost everything I had typed.
It has been reloading for two minutes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reload the page), intransitive (the page reloaded by itself)

entries.meaning: To switch a setting on or off, or to move back and forth between two options. ---
examples: Toggle dark mode in the settings menu.
He toggled the switch and the screen went black.
She was toggling between two spreadsheets all morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (toggle the setting), intransitive (toggle between the two views)
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: toggling.

entries.meaning: To make a file smaller so that it takes less space or sends faster. ---
examples: Compress the folder before you email it.
He compressed the video and lost some quality.
The app is compressing two hundred photos.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ss: compresses.

entries.meaning: To pull files or data out of an archive or a larger set. ---
examples: Extract the folder to your desktop.
The tool extracted every email address from the page.
It is extracting three thousand files.
entries.contrast: The verb is ik-STRAKT; the noun extract (a short passage) is EK-strakt.

entries.meaning: To turn data into code so that only the right person can read it. ---
examples: Encrypt the folder before you put it in the cloud.
The app encrypted the messages end to end.
All of our backups are encrypted.

entries.meaning: To turn coded data back into a readable form. ---
examples: Only the key can decrypt the file.
They decrypted the message in under an hour.
The program is decrypting the archive now.

entries.meaning: To list and organize data so that it can be searched quickly. ---
examples: Search engines index millions of pages a day.
Google indexed the new site within a week.
The database is still indexing.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -x: indexes.

entries.meaning: To ask a database or a system for particular information. ---
examples: You can query the database straight from the browser.
He queried the server and got an empty result.
The script is querying three tables at once.
entries.contrast: Consonant + y, so the y changes: queries, queried. The -ing form keeps it: querying.

entries.meaning: To store data for a short time so that it loads faster the next time. ---
examples: Browsers cache images to save time.
The page was cached, so I saw yesterday's price.
The app is caching the whole playlist.
entries.contrast: Cache is pronounced exactly like cash, not ka-SHAY.

entries.meaning: To put a video, a map, or a piece of code inside a page or a document. ---
examples: You can embed the video right in the post.
She embedded a map on the contact page.
He is embedding the font in the file.
entries.contrast: Double the d: embedded, embedding.

entries.meaning: To turn paper documents, photos, or tapes into computer files. ---
examples: The library wants to digitize every old map.
We digitized the family videos last summer.
They have been digitizing records since 2019.
entries.contrast: American -ize; British writing has digitise.

entries.meaning: To break the link between a device and a network or another device. ---
examples: Disconnect the drive before you pull the cable.
The call disconnected after two minutes.
My laptop keeps disconnecting from the Wi-Fi.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (disconnect the drive), intransitive (my phone keeps disconnecting)
entries.contrast: You disconnect FROM a network.

entries.meaning: To join a device or a call back to a network after it was cut off. ---
examples: Try to reconnect to the other network.
He reconnected the printer and it worked again.
The app is reconnecting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reconnect the printer), intransitive (the call reconnected on its own)

entries.meaning: To pull a plug or a cable out of a socket or a device. ---
examples: Unplug the router for ten seconds.
Someone unplugged the monitor.
He is unplugging every cable to find the bad one.
entries.русский: отключать от сети, отключить; выдёргивать из розетки
entries.contrast: Double the g: unplugged, unplugging.

entries.meaning: To fill a battery with power again. ---
examples: Recharge the battery overnight.
I recharged the headphones in the car.
The power bank is recharging.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (recharge the battery), intransitive (the case recharges in an hour)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ge: recharges.

entries.meaning: To supply a device with the electricity it needs to run. ---
examples: Two small batteries power the whole sensor.
The old model was powered by a wall adapter.
One cable is powering both screens.
entries.contrast: Power up and power down are separate phrasal verbs.

entries.meaning: To change from one thing, setting, or service to another. ---
examples: Switch the phone to airplane mode.
We switched to a cheaper carrier last year.
She is switching between four browser tabs.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (switch the setting), intransitive (we switched to a new provider)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: switches. You switch TO a new plan and switch FROM the old one.

entries.meaning: To start a computer so that the operating system loads. ---
examples: The old tower takes a full minute to boot.
He booted the laptop from a USB stick.
The machine is still booting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (boot the machine from a USB drive), intransitive (the laptop boots in ten seconds)

entries.meaning: To start a computer or device again after shutting it down. ---
examples: Reboot the router and try again.
I rebooted the laptop three times.
The server is rebooting.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reboot the router), intransitive (the server rebooted overnight)

entries.meaning: To stop a program or a device and start it again right away. ---
examples: Restart the app after the update.
She restarted the computer and the error disappeared.
It has been restarting for five minutes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (restart the app), intransitive (the phone restarted by itself)

entries.meaning: To broadcast an event over the internet while it is happening. ---
examples: They livestream every home game.
She livestreamed the wedding for relatives abroad.
He is livestreaming from the parking lot.
entries.русский: вести прямую трансляцию, транслировать в прямом эфире
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (livestream the ceremony), intransitive (she livestreams every Friday)
entries.contrast: Written as one word or as live-stream; both are common. The first part rhymes with five, not with give.

entries.meaning: To load part of a video or a song in advance so that it plays without stopping. ---
examples: A weak connection makes every video buffer.
The stream buffered twice during the final.
It keeps buffering right at the good part.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the player buffers a few seconds of video), intransitive (the stream keeps buffering)

entries.meaning: To respond slowly, so that the picture or the sound falls behind. ---
examples: The video will lag on this connection.
The audio lagged about half a second behind.
My screen is lagging badly today.
entries.contrast: Double the g: lagged, lagging.

entries.meaning: To send data or a signal from one place to another. ---
examples: The sensor can transmit data over a mile.
The station transmitted the warning at noon.
The device has been transmitting all night.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (transmit the data), intransitive (the beacon transmits every hour)
entries.contrast: Double the t: transmitted, transmitting - the stress falls on the last syllable.

entries.meaning: To send data, calls, or traffic along a particular path. ---
examples: The system routes every call through one server.
They routed the traffic around the damaged cable.
It is routing my request to the wrong office.
entries.contrast: Most Americans say ROOT, like the root of a tree; ROWT is also heard. The -ing form keeps the e: routing.

entries.meaning: To send a short signal or message to a device or a person. ---
examples: Ping me when the file is ready.
I pinged the server and got no answer.
My phone has been pinging every two minutes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (ping me when you land), intransitive (the phone pings all day)

entries.meaning: To show the picture from one screen on another, or to keep an identical copy of data. ---
examples: You can mirror your phone to the TV.
He mirrored the laptop screen onto the projector.
The second drive is mirroring everything in real time.

entries.meaning: To connect a computer to the internet through a phone's data connection. ---
examples: You can tether the laptop to your phone.
He tethered for a week while the cable was out.
She is tethering from her phone right now.
entries.русский: раздавать интернет с телефона, использовать телефон как модем
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tether the laptop to your phone), intransitive (we tethered all week)
entries.contrast: You tether one device TO another.

entries.meaning: To remove a program from a computer or a phone. ---
examples: Uninstall the app and install it again.
I uninstalled three games to free up space.
It is uninstalling the old version now.
entries.contrast: The base already ends in -ll, so the forms look heavy but are regular: uninstalled, uninstalling.

entries.meaning: To install a program or a system again after removing it. ---
examples: Reinstall the driver and reboot.
He reinstalled the whole operating system.
She has reinstalled the app twice today.

entries.meaning: To move to a lower, cheaper, or older version of software or a plan. ---
examples: You can downgrade the plan at any time.
He downgraded to the free account.
They are downgrading the software to last year's build.
entries.русский: понижать версию, понизить; переходить на более дешёвый тариф
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (downgrade the software), intransitive (we downgraded to the free plan)
entries.contrast: The opposite of upgrade. Drop the -e before -ing: downgrading.

entries.meaning: To find and fix the errors in a program. ---
examples: It takes longer to debug the code than to write it.
She debugged the payment form in one afternoon.
He has been debugging the same function for days.
entries.русский: отлаживать, отладить; искать и исправлять ошибки
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (debug the code), intransitive (he debugs all day)
entries.contrast: Double the g: debugged, debugging.

entries.meaning: To use a computer to copy the way something works in real life. ---
examples: The program can simulate a whole flight.
They simulated the crash a thousand times.
The lab is simulating next week's storm.

entries.meaning: To make one system behave exactly like another. ---
examples: This app can emulate an old game console.
The software emulated Windows well enough to run the program.
It is emulating a printer that no longer exists.

entries.meaning: To work out a result by calculation, usually with a machine. ---
examples: The server can compute the route in a second.
The model computed a ninety percent chance of rain.
It is computing the totals for all fifty states.

entries.meaning: To change something so that it works as well or as fast as possible. ---
examples: Optimize the images or the page will crawl.
They optimized the app for older phones.
He has been optimizing the database all week.
entries.contrast: American -ize; British writing has optimise.

entries.meaning: To change something in size, or to grow so as to handle much more work. ---
examples: The design has to scale to any screen size.
They scaled the service to ten million users.
The company is scaling faster than it can hire.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scale the image), intransitive (the service scales to millions of users)
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: scaling.

entries.meaning: To make two systems work together as one. ---
examples: The app can integrate with your calendar.
They integrated the payment system last month.
We are integrating the two databases.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (integrate the two systems), intransitive (the app integrates with your calendar)
entries.contrast: Integrate WITH another system, or integrate one thing INTO another.

entries.meaning: To set up a device or a program so that it works the way you want. ---
examples: Configure the printer before you leave.
He configured the router for the whole office.
She is configuring the new laptops.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: configuring.

entries.meaning: To change settings or content so that they fit one particular person. ---
examples: You can personalize the home screen.
The store personalized every email with my name.
The app is personalizing your feed.

entries.meaning: To build a rough first version of a product in order to test the idea. ---
examples: We can prototype the app in a week.
They prototyped three different layouts.
She is prototyping the checkout screen.

entries.meaning: To create new methods, ideas, or products. ---
examples: Small teams often innovate faster than big ones.
The company innovated early and took the market.
They have been innovating in battery design for years.

entries.meaning: To open or reach data, a file, or an account. ---
examples: You can access the files from any device.
Someone accessed my account from another country.
He is accessing the server remotely.
entries.русский: получать доступ, получить доступ; заходить, зайти (в систему)
entries.contrast: The verb takes a direct object: access the file. Only the noun takes to: access to the file.

entries.meaning: To prove that a user or a device is who it claims to be. ---
examples: The app will authenticate you with your fingerprint.
The system authenticated the login in a second.
It is authenticating your device now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (authenticate the user), intransitive (the device authenticates in a second)

entries.meaning: To check that data or a document is correct and acceptable. ---
examples: The form will validate the email address.
The system validated the card and charged it.
It is validating the file against the template.

entries.meaning: To stop something from being used or changed without a key, a code, or a password. ---
examples: Lock your screen when you leave the desk.
He locked the file so that nobody could edit it.
The phone is locking itself every thirty seconds.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (lock the screen), intransitive (the phone locks after a minute)

entries.meaning: To open something that was locked, or to make a hidden feature available. ---
examples: Unlock the phone with your face.
She unlocked the front door from the app.
Finishing the level has unlocked two new maps.

entries.meaning: To make a service, a card, or a feature start working. ---
examples: Activate the SIM card before your flight.
He activated the alarm from his phone.
They are activating the new accounts today.

entries.meaning: To turn off an account or a feature so that it stops working. ---
examples: You can deactivate the account without deleting it.
She deactivated her profile for a month.
He is deactivating the old key cards.

entries.meaning: To turn a setting or a feature on. ---
examples: Enable two-factor login in the settings.
I enabled notifications and now the phone never stops.
Location sharing has been enabled by default.
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: enabling.

entries.meaning: To turn a setting or a feature off. ---
examples: Disable the pop-ups and the site is readable.
He disabled the camera in the settings.
The update has disabled my printer.

entries.meaning: To send someone a lot of unwanted messages. ---
examples: Please do not spam the group chat.
They spammed every address on the list.
He is spamming the comments with links.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (spam the group chat), intransitive (they spam all day)
entries.contrast: Double the m: spammed, spamming.

entries.meaning: To turn off the sound of a device, a call, or a conversation. ---
examples: Mute yourself when you are not speaking.
He muted the group chat for a week.
She is muting every notification before bed.
entries.русский: выключать звук, выключить звук; отключать уведомления
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: muting.

entries.meaning: To turn the sound back on. ---
examples: Unmute yourself - we cannot hear you.
He unmuted the call and his dog was barking.
She has unmuted the thread.

entries.meaning: To stop receiving emails or content from a service you signed up for. ---
examples: Unsubscribe at the bottom of the email.
I unsubscribed from forty newsletters in one evening.
He has unsubscribed and the mail still keeps coming.
entries.contrast: You unsubscribe FROM a list.

entries.meaning: To enter a phone number in order to make a call. ---
examples: Dial the extension after the beep.
He dialed the wrong number twice.
She is dialing in from the airport.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dial the number), intransitive (dial slowly)
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: dialed, dialing. British writing has dialled, dialling.

entries.meaning: To look something up on the internet with a search engine. ---
examples: Google it before you call support.
I googled the error message and found the fix.
He was googling her name the whole flight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (google the address), intransitive (just google and see)
entries.contrast: As a verb it is written in lowercase, and the -e is dropped: googling.

entries.meaning: To move from page to page on the internet with no fixed goal. ---
examples: They surf the web instead of working.
She surfed the net until two in the morning.
He has been surfing real estate listings all week.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (surf the web), intransitive (he surfed for hours)

entries.meaning: To save a picture of what is on your screen. ---
examples: Screenshot the confirmation page.
She screenshotted the whole conversation.
He is screenshotting every message as proof.
entries.contrast: Double the t: screenshotted, screenshotting. In formal writing, take a screenshot is safer.

entries.meaning: To put items in order by importance, or to hold a place in such an order. ---
examples: Search engines rank pages by hundreds of signals.
The site ranked third for that keyword.
The app is ranking higher every month.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the algorithm ranks the results), intransitive (the site ranks first)

entries.meaning: To warn someone about something quickly. ---
examples: The app will alert you when the price drops.
The system alerted the whole team at 3 a.m.
It has been alerting us every hour since then.
entries.contrast: You alert someone TO a problem.

entries.meaning: To ask a user on screen to do something, or to give a system an instruction. ---
examples: The site will prompt you for a code.
It prompted me to change my password.
The app keeps prompting me to rate it.
entries.contrast: Prompt someone TO do something, or prompt someone FOR information.

entries.meaning: To act on each other, or to communicate with a person or a system. ---
examples: Children interact with screens before they can read.
The two programs interacted badly and the system froze.
He has been interacting with customers all day.
entries.contrast: You interact WITH someone or something.

entries.meaning: To fail or behave strangely for a short time. ---
examples: Cheap screens glitch in the cold.
The payment page glitched and charged me twice.
The video keeps glitching at the same spot.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: glitches.

entries.meaning: To become, or to make something become, too hot to work safely. ---
examples: Old laptops overheat under any real load.
The phone overheated in the car.
The battery is overheating again.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the sun overheated the phone), intransitive (the laptop overheats)

entries.meaning: To make a disk or a drive come out safely. ---
examples: Eject the drive before you pull it out.
He ejected the card and the photos were gone.
The laptop is ejecting the disc.

entries.meaning: To break the connection between two accounts, files, or devices. ---
examples: Unlink the card before you close the account.
He unlinked his email from the old profile.
She has unlinked every app from her calendar.

entries.meaning: To put songs, cards, or files into a random order. ---
examples: Shuffle the playlist - I know it by heart.
The app shuffled the same five songs all night.
It is shuffling my whole library.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (shuffle the playlist), intransitive (the app shuffles automatically)
entries.contrast: Drop the -e before -ing: shuffling.

entries.meaning: To connect computers or devices so that they can share data.
examples: We can network all four printers.
They networked the two offices last year.
Every machine is networked through one switch.
entries.русский: объединять в сеть, объединить в сеть
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (network the office printers), intransitive (the machines network over Wi-Fi)
